To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the signal recognition particle is not required for the translocation of a subset of pre-proteins in yeast, that the signal sequences of preprotein can be used to predict the targeting pathway that will be used, and that the targeting pathway used by a preprotein is determined by a specific structural feature of the signal sequence.
the SRP-independent pathway is used by the majority of secretory and ER membrane proteins, and that the hydrophobicity of signal sequences specifies the pathway used for targeting.

(1) SRP-independent targeting is a distinct pathway that can be distinguished from SRP-dependent targeting by its dependence on SEC62 and SEC62, and (2) SRP-dependent and SRP-independent targeting are distinguished by the hydrophobility of the signal sequence.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanism of targeting proteins to the endoplamic reticulum.
the mechanisms by which proteins are targeted to the endoplamic reticulum.
the mechanism by which the ER translocates preproteins.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
signal sequences are not just a means of targeting to the ER membrane but also a means to specify the pathway taken.
the signal recognition particle pathway is not the only one in the cell, but rather that it is one of two pathways that can be used by preproteins to reach the endoplasmically reticular membrane.
the SRP-independent targeting pathway is not a default pathway, but a distinct, independent pathway.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
signal sequences specify the targeting pathway as well as the membrane insertion site.
signal sequences are more diverse in their function than previously appreciated, and that the SRP-independent pathway is not a default pathway for the translocation of all ER-directed preproteins.
there are two targeting pathways to the ER membrane, one that is SRP dependent and another that is SRP independent.
The main takeaway from our work is that
signal sequences can be classified into three groups, SRP-dependent, SRP-independent, or dual.
there are two distinct pathways to the ER, and that the signal sequence determines whether a protein is translocated by one or both of these routes.
there are two targeting pathways in yeast that function independently.
